response.title: How many solar panels does it take to refill a home backup battery in one winter day in a northern state?
response.answer:
For a typical home backup battery in a northern U.S. state such as Minnesota, Michigan, or Wisconsin, you'd need approximately 20–40 solar panels (400W each) to fully recharge a 13.5 kWh battery in one average winter day.

The number varies dramatically with weather, battery size, and whether your home is consuming electricity while charging.

How many panels do you need?

Assuming a 400W panel, about 80% overall system efficiency, and 1.5–2.5 peak sun hours per winter day:

The biggest challenge: cloudy winter days

NREL solar modeling shows that Minneapolis can receive around 2–3 peak sun hours on an average December day, depending on panel tilt. 
NREL

But during a multi-day winter storm, output can fall dramatically. Snow covering the panels can stop production almost entirely.

For reliable winter backup, sizing for an average day isn't enough. You may need extra battery capacity, a generator, or grid charging to survive several consecutive low-sun days.

One question that would help narrow this down: Are you trying to recharge a single 10–15 kWh battery (like a Tesla Powerwall), or a larger 30–50 kWh whole-home battery system?
markup:
For a typical home backup battery in a northern U.S. state such as Minnesota, Michigan, or Wisconsin, you'd need approximately **20–40 solar panels (400W each)** to fully recharge a 13.5 kWh battery in one average winter day.

The number varies dramatically with weather, battery size, and whether your home is consuming electricity while charging.

## How many panels do you need?

Assuming a 400W panel, about 80% overall system efficiency, and 1.5–2.5 peak sun hours per winter day:

| Battery capacity | Panels needed |
|---|---:|
| 5 kWh | 7–11 |
| 10 kWh | 13–21 |
| 13.5 kWh (Tesla Powerwall size) | 17–29 |
| 20 kWh | 25–42 |
| 30 kWh | 38–63 |
| 40 kWh | 50–84 |

These estimates assume the battery starts empty, the solar energy goes entirely toward charging, and the panels are unshaded and free of snow.

## Calculate it for your situation

{@body const [capacity,setCapacity] = DIL.useState(13.5)}
{@body const [sun,setSun] = DIL.useState("2")}
{@body const [panel,setPanel] = DIL.useState("400")}
{@body const [load,setLoad] = DIL.useState("0")}
{@body const count = Math.ceil((capacity+Number(load))/(Number(panel)/1000*Number(sun)*0.8))}
<box border radius="2xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Battery capacity**
    <title size="lg" color="default" tabularNums>{capacity} kWh</title>
  </row>
  <slider min={5} max={50} step={0.5} value={capacity} onChange={setCapacity}/>
  <label>Solar panel wattage</label>
  <radio-group value={panel} onChange={setPanel} direction="row">
    <radio value="400">400W</radio>
    <radio value="450">450W</radio>
    <radio value="500">500W</radio>
  </radio-group>
  <label>Winter sunlight conditions</label>
  <radio-group direction="col" value={sun} onChange={setSun}>
    <radio value="3">Good winter day — 3 peak sun hours</radio>
    <radio value="2">Average winter day — 2 peak sun hours</radio>
    <radio value="0.5">Very cloudy day — 0.5 peak sun hours</radio>
  </radio-group>
  <label>Home electricity usage during charging</label>
  <radio-group direction="col" value={load} onChange={setLoad}>
    <radio value="0">None — all solar goes to battery</radio>
    <radio value="5">5 kWh</radio>
    <radio value="10">10 kWh</radio>
    <radio value="20">20 kWh</radio>
  </radio-group>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="xl" padding={3} gap={1}>
    <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">Estimated panels required</text>
    <row align="baseline" gap={2}>
      <title size="2xl" color="default" tabularNums>{count}</title>
      <text color="secondary">panels</text>
    </row>
    <text color="secondary" size="sm">{(count*Number(panel)/1000).toFixed(1)} kW solar array · approximately {((capacity+Number(load))/Number(sun)/0.8).toFixed(1)} kW required</text>
  </box>
</box>

## The biggest challenge: cloudy winter days

NREL solar modeling shows that Minneapolis can receive around 2–3 peak sun hours on an average December day, depending on panel tilt. <Cite ref="turn426557search12"/>

But during a multi-day winter storm, output can fall dramatically. Snow covering the panels can stop production almost entirely.

**For reliable winter backup, sizing for an average day isn't enough.** You may need extra battery capacity, a generator, or grid charging to survive several consecutive low-sun days.

One question that would help narrow this down: **Are you trying to recharge a single 10–15 kWh battery (like a Tesla Powerwall), or a larger 30–50 kWh whole-home battery system?**
